title: How many friends do you really have?

fn.en: Talk about friendships and about things that are changing right now.

gr: the present simple, continuous and perfect together

can.en: I can talk about my friendships and about what is changing right now.

useful: We don’t have much in common, but…
We’ve fallen out, so we’re not speaking at the moment
rc: the present perfect with for and since

acts.say: Say which column your own friendships mostly live in.

items.q: I don’t know her well enough to ___ her with my problems.
Our ___ started in the first week of university and it is still going.

items.why: media is a noun for newspapers, television and the internet; the other three are time adverbs.

items.q: Which one does NOT belong with the others?
items.why: fall out means to stop being friendly; the other three bring people together.

items.q: Which one is NOT a noun?
Which one would you NOT expect in a sentence about your free time?
Which one is NOT a thing you can be a member of?

sub.en: Look at the time words in each sentence — they decide the form.

items.q: Alan ___ well with almost everybody at work.
items.why: A general truth about somebody takes the present simple.

items.q: I can’t come tonight — I ___ Dana for coffee at eight.
items.why: A fixed arrangement in the near future takes the present continuous.

items.q: Sam and I ___ friends since primary school.
items.why: RECYCLED from Pre-Intermediate: since fixes the start of something that is still true, so the present perfect is used.

items.q: How long ___ Jem?
items.why: How long asks about a period up to now, so the present perfect is used. know is also a state verb.

items.q: The internet ___ the way we make friends — the process is still going on.
items.why: The present continuous shows a change in progress around now.

items.q: I ___ three people from my old school this month.
items.why: this month is not finished, so the present perfect counts what has happened so far.

items.q: ___ much at the weekend, or do you stay in?
items.why: A habit — how often something usually happens — takes the present simple.

items.q: She ___ me a lot lately.
items.why: lately points to a period running up to now, so the present perfect is used.

lines: Sam and I [have been|are being|were] friends since we were eleven.
We don’t see each other often, but we [text|are texting|have texted] each other every week.
Right now he [is living|lives|has lived] in Astana, and I [am staying|have stayed|stay] here.
I [haven’t seen|don’t see|am not seeing] him since March, but we [are meeting|meet|have met] up next month.
To be honest, our friendship [has improved|improves|improved] a lot this year.

items.from: Aigul and I met in 2019. We are still friends.
items.cue: Join it into one sentence with since
items.a: Aigul and I have been friends since 2019

items.from: I know Jem. We met ten years ago.
items.cue: Ask about the length of the friendship
items.a: How long have you known Jem

items.from: Your plan for Friday: coffee with Dana.
items.a: I am meeting Dana on Friday

items.from: Every Saturday: football with the same group.
items.a: I play football with them every Saturday

items.from: Our communication is getting better and better.
I last fell out with somebody in 2020.
items.a: I have not fallen out with anybody since 2020

items.from: I started using this app three years ago.
items.cue: Rewrite it with FOR. Begin: I have…
items.a: I have used this app for three years
alt: I’ve used this app for three years
I have been using this app for three years
I’ve been using this app for three years
items.why: for + a length of time; since + the point when it started.

items.cue: Rewrite it with SINCE. Begin: We have…

items.from: Dana and I are not speaking to each other. It started last month.
items.cue: Put it in one sentence with SINCE.
items.a: Dana and I have not spoken to each other since last month
alt: Dana and I haven’t spoken to each other since last month
Dana and I have not spoken since last month
Dana and I haven’t spoken since last month

items.from: When did you meet your closest friend?
items.cue: Ask about the length of the friendship. Use KNOWN.
items.a: How long have you known your closest friend

items.from: My brother is in London. He went there in June.
items.cue: Put it in one sentence with SINCE.
items.a: My brother has been in London since June

items.from: I don’t use that site now. I stopped in 2021.
items.cue: Rewrite it with NOT … SINCE. Begin: I have…
items.a: I have not used that site since 2021
alt: I haven’t used that site since 2021

items.why: since marks the start of something still true now, so the present perfect is needed.
for + a length of time (two years); since + a point in time (2015, June, Monday).
know is a state verb and is not normally used in the continuous.
A repeated habit takes the present simple.
last Friday is finished time, so the past simple is used.
this month is unfinished, so the present perfect reports the result so far.

tts: So, how many friends would you say you have?
It depends what you mean by friends. I get on well with about twenty people at work — I would call them friends.
Do you socialize outside work?
Not that often, but we meet up after work from time to time. Then there are the people I play football with. I don’t have much in common with them apart from football.
And how many of them would you ask to help you out if you were in trouble?
Ah, that is different. Friends you can really trust — maybe five or six.
What about online?
I have got about fifteen or twenty, but I hardly use it. What about you?
I have about a hundred and fifty. We send each other the occasional message.
Have you actually met all of them?
No. Some of them I have never met at all.
And in real life?

I have friends from work, and people from my evening class — I am learning German at the moment. But I have only got a couple of really close friends. Actually, currently just one, because I have fallen out with one of my best friends.

write.q: Write about two of your friendships. Use one present simple sentence (what you usually do together), one present continuous sentence (what is changing, or an arrangement), and two present perfect sentences with for or since.
plan: what is different at the moment
write.model: I’ve known Aigul since university — that’s about twelve years. We don’t have a lot in common, but we get on well. We usually meet up for coffee once a month, and we text almost every week. At the moment we’re seeing each other less, because she’s working nights. I’m meeting her for lunch on Saturday, and I haven’t seen her since March.

speak.q: Talk for about a minute about your closest friend: how long you have known them, what you usually do together, and what is happening in the friendship right now.
speak.model: My closest friend is Marat. We’ve been friends since we were eleven — we were at the same school. We don’t see each other every week, but we keep in touch, and he always helps me out when something goes wrong. Right now we’re both very busy, so we’re meeting up less than usual. Actually, I’m seeing him on Friday.
